editorial.headline: Urban Tourist Rail Transport: Open Nationally, Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This urban tourist rail activity is open to foreign investment nationally, with full foreign ownership permitted and no Bali moratorium block for PMA registration.
editorial.body:
This activity is the operation of tourist trains that run on dedicated tracks as part of urban transport. Its setting is a tourism area, and its transport logic remains urban: the service operates within a city transport context. The record’s own illustration is a cable car serving a tourism precinct. That example keeps the focus on the operational fact that matters here—the running of rail-based tourist transport on a special route within an urban network. The definition puts three elements side by side: an operator of the service, the dedicated route it uses, and the urban-tourism setting in which it moves people. Those elements should remain visible when a business describes what it intends to register.

Who may register it is equally defined by scale. The record opens this activity to medium and large enterprises, so the business profile should be built around one of those two stated scales rather than an assumed smaller category. At national level it is marked open to foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. This is not merely a broad invitation to tourism businesses: it is the ownership position attached to the described operating activity. A founder or investor therefore has a clear national reading: foreign capital can enter, and the stated ceiling allows full foreign ownership. The record cites Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as its national source. The important editorial discipline is to keep that national position attached to this activity’s particular scope and stated scales, not turn it into a claim about a wider transport or tourism market.

Bali changes the question from what foreign ownership is permitted nationally to whether provincial policy blocks PMA registration. Here the answer is clean: it does not. Bali’s result is recorded as OK or higher risk, and this activity is not blocked by the province-wide, permanent PMA moratorium. The accompanying reason is specific: at the Large scale, its OSS risk is Medium-High/High, and it is therefore not blocked by that moratorium. That is a Bali-side risk classification, not a second foreign-ownership percentage or a local-partnership requirement; neither is supplied in the record. For an investor assessing this exact activity, the honest combined reading is straightforward. Nationally, the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%; in Bali, PMA registration is not stopped by the stated moratorium. The large-scale risk label is still part of the Bali picture and should be read as such—present, explicit, and not a reason to invent further conditions.
